{{Short description|Figure-eight-shaped curve on a sphere}}
[[File:Viviani-fenster-1.svg|thumb|Viviani's curve: intersection of a sphere with a tangent cylinder.]]
[[File:Viviani-fenster-2.svg|thumb|upright=0.75|The light blue part of the hemisphere can be squared.]]
In [[mathematics]], '''Viviani's curve''', also known as '''Viviani's window''', is a [[Lemniscate|figure-eight-shaped]] space [[curve]] named after the Italian mathematician [[Vincenzo Viviani]]. It is the intersection of a [[sphere]] with a [[cylinder (geometry)|cylinder]] that is [[tangent]] to the sphere and passes through two poles (a diameter) of the sphere (see diagram). Before Viviani, this curve was studied by [[Simon de la Loubère|Simon de La Loubère]] and [[Gilles de Roberval]].<ref>Kuno Fladt: ''Analytische Geometrie spezieller Flächen und Raumkurven.'' Springer-Verlag, 2013, {{ISBN|3322853659}}, 9783322853653, p. 97.</ref><ref>[[Karl Strubecker|K. Strubecker]]: ''Vorlesungen der Darstellenden Geometrie.'' Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, Göttingen 1967, p. 250.</ref>

The [[orthographic projection]] of Viviani's curve onto a plane perpendicular to the line through the crossing point and the sphere center is the [[lemniscate of Gerono]], while the [[stereographic projection]] is a hyperbola or the [[lemniscate of Bernoulli]], depending on which point on the same line is used to project.<ref>{{citation|first1=Luisa Rossi|last1=Costa|first2=Elena|last2=Marchetti|contribution=Mathematical and Historical Investigation on Domes and Vaults|pages=73–80|title=Aesthetics and architectural composition : proceedings of the Dresden International Symposium of Architecture 2004|year=2005|location=Mammendorf|publisher=Pro Literatur|editor1-last=Weber|editor1-first=Ralf|editor2-last=Amann|editor2-first=Matthias Albrecht}}.</ref>

In 1692, Viviani solved the following task: Cut out of a hemisphere (radius <math>r</math>) two windows, such that the remaining surface (of the hemisphere) can be [[Squaring the circle|''squared'']]; that is, a [[square]] with the same area can be constructed [[Straightedge and compass construction|using only ruler and compass]]. His solution has an area of <math>4r^2</math> (see below).

== Equations ==
[[File:Viviani_kromme.jpg|thumb|With the cylinder upright.]] 
In order to keep the proof for squaring simple, suppose that the sphere and cylinder have the equations
: <math>x^2+y^2+z^2=r^2</math>
and
: <math>x^2+y^2-rx=0,</math>
respectively.  The cylinder has radius <math>r/2</math> and is tangent to the sphere at point <math>(r,0,0).</math>

== Properties of the curve ==
=== Floor plan, elevation, and side plan ===
[[File:Viviani-fenster-xyz.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|Floor plan, elevation and side plan]]
Elimination of <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>, and <math>z</math> respectively yields the [[orthogonal projection|orthogonal projections]] of the intersection curve onto the:
: <math>x</math>-<math>y</math>-plane is the ''circle'' with equation <math>\left(x-\tfrac{r}{2} \right)^2+y^2  = \left(\tfrac{r}{2} \right)^2,</math>
: <math>x</math>-<math>z</math>-plane the ''[[parabola]]'' with equation <math>x=-\tfrac{1}{r}z^2+r,</math> and
: <math>y</math>-<math>z</math>-plane the [[algebraic curve]] with the equation <math>z^4+r^2(y^2-z^2)=0.</math>

=== Parametric representation ===
[[File:Viviani-fenster-3.svg|thumb|For parametric representation and the determination of the area]]
Representing the sphere by 
: <math>\begin{array}{cll}
x &=& r \cdot \cos \theta \cdot \cos \varphi \\
y &=& r \cdot \cos \theta \cdot \sin \varphi \\
z &=& r \cdot \sin \theta \qquad \qquad -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \ -\pi\le\varphi\le \pi,
\end{array}</math>
and setting <math>\varphi=\theta, </math> yields the curve 
: <math>
\begin{array}{cll}
x &=& r \cdot \cos \theta \cdot \cos \theta \\
y &=& r \cdot \cos \theta \cdot \sin \theta \\
z &=& r \cdot \sin \theta \qquad \qquad -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\tfrac{\pi}{2}.
\end{array}
</math>

One easily checks that the spherical curve fulfills the equation of the cylinder. But the boundaries allow only the red part (see diagram) of Viviani's curve. The missing second half (green) has the property <math>\varphi=-\theta.</math>

With help of this parametric representation it is easy to prove that the area of the hemisphere containing Viviani's curve minus the area of the two windows is <math>4r^2</math>. The area of the upper-right part of Viviani's window (see diagram) can be calculated by an [[Surface integral|integration]]:
:<math>\iint_{S_{sphere}} r^2 \cos\theta \,\mathrm{d}\theta\, \mathrm{d}\varphi =r^2 \int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^\theta \cos\theta \,\mathrm{d}\varphi \,\mathrm{d}\theta= r^2 \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-1 \right).
</math>
Hence the total area of the spherical surface included by Viviani's curve is <math>2\pi r^2-4r^2</math>, and the area of the hemisphere (<math>2\pi r^2</math>) minus the area of Viviani's window is <math>4r^2</math>, the area of a square with the sphere's diameter as the length of an edge.

=== Rational Bézier representation ===
The quarter of Viviani's curve that lies in the all-positive [[Octant (solid geometry)|octant]] of 3D space cannot be represented exactly by a regular [[Bézier curve]] of any degree.  However, it can be represented exactly by a 3D rational Bézier segment of degree 4, and there is an infinite family of rational Bézier control points generating that segment.  One possible solution is given by the following five control points:

<math>p_0 = (0, 0, 1, 1)</math>

<math>\begin{array}{llllll}
p_0 & = & (0 & 0 & 1 & 1) & & \\
p_1 & = & (0 & 1 & 2 & 2) &/& (2\sqrt{2}) \\
p_2 & = & (2 & 3 & 3 & 4) &/& 6 \\
p_3 & = & (2 & 1 & 1 & 2) &/& (2\sqrt{2}) \\
p_4 & = & (1 & 0 & 0 & 1) & &
\end{array}</math>

:<math>
\boldsymbol{p0} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
\boldsymbol{p1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}
\boldsymbol{p2} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{2}{3} \end{bmatrix}
\boldsymbol{p3} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}
\boldsymbol{p4} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
</math>

The corresponding rational parametrization is:
:<math>
\left(
\begin{array}{c}
\displaystyle \frac{2 \mu ^2 \left(\mu ^2-2 \left(2+\sqrt{2}\right) \mu +4 \sqrt{2}+6\right)}{\left(2 (\mu -1)
   \mu +\sqrt{2}+2\right)^2} \\
\displaystyle \frac{2 (\mu -1) \mu  \left((\mu -1) \mu -3 \sqrt{2}-4\right)}{\left(2 (\mu -1) \mu
   +\sqrt{2}+2\right)^2} \\
\displaystyle -\frac{(\mu -1) \left(\sqrt{2} \mu +\sqrt{2}+2\right)}{2 (\mu -1) \mu +\sqrt{2}+2} \\
\end{array}
\right) \; \mu\in\left[0,1\right]
</math>

== Relation to other curves ==
* The 8-shaped elevation (see above) is a [[Lemniscate of Gerono]].
* Viviani's curve is a special [[Clelia curve]]. For a Clelia curve, the relation between the angles is <math>\varphi=c\theta.</math>

[[File:Viviani-kugel-kegel.svg|thumb|Viviani's curve (red) as intersection of the sphere and a cone (pink)]]
Subtracting twice the cylinder equation from the sphere's equation and [[completing the square]] leads to the equation
:<math>(x-r)^2+y^2=z^2,</math>
which describes a [[right circular cone]] with its apex at <math>(r,0,0)</math>, the [[double point]] of Viviani's curve. Hence, Viviani's curve can be considered not only as the intersection curve of a sphere and a cylinder but also as the intersection of a sphere and a cone, and as the intersection of a cylinder and a cone.
